newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait minister slams MP critics over violations.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait minister slams MP critics over violations.

text.p: Kuwait's finance minister on Tuesday slammed critics over alleged corruption in state institutions and said questions in parliament were aimed at forcing the government to resign.
"The target is not the finance minister but bringing down the government," Nasser al-Rodhan told parliament.

Rodhan, first made finance minister in 1991 shortly after the Gulf War over Iraq's occupation of Kuwait, is facing questioning in parliament over alleged violations by institutions that fall under his jurisdiction.
He chairs the Kuwait Investment Authority (KIA), which manages the state's foreign investments of more than $40 billion, the Central Bank and Kuwait Airways.
Rodhan said the questioning document contained more than 50 accusations, using language "which should not be used in parliamentary work...Today we are before strange questioning.
"This is a good opportunity for me to prove that I entered the cabinet with a clean white robe which, with God's help, will always remain clean."
He then responded to each of the 10 issues presented in his questioning by three opposition MPs.
Earlier on Tuesday opposition MP Sami al-Munayes, one of the MPs who signed the request, listed financial transactions which allegedly cost the state tens of millions of dollars.
Munayes claimed that corruption was rampant due to lack of measures to montior public funds and failure to conduct adequate checks when appointing officials in charge of state funds.
Rodhan's questioning, the 12th since Kuwait's first parliament in 1963, is the first of a cabinet minister by the parliament which was elected in October.
Rodhan's opponents need 10 votes for a no-confidence motion which then requires the support of 24 of 46 elected MPs to force the minister to resign. Four other elected MPs are ministers.
The government has backed Rodhan, who also enjoys the support of some pro-government MPs while liberal and Moslem Shi'ite groupings appear ready to push for a no-confidence vote.
Other groupings have said they would decide their final position after listening to Rodhan's response to the charges.
Kuwait, the only Gulf Arab state with an elected parliament, has no political parties.
